title: “DO NOT GIVE DOGS WHAT IS HOLY” — ONE OF JESUS’ STRANGEST AND MOST IGNORED COMMANDS
paragraphs: “DO NOT GIVE DOGS WHAT IS HOLY” — ONE OF JESUS’ STRANGEST AND MOST IGNORED COMMANDS

Jesus told you to love your enemies. He told you not to judge hypocritically. But then He said something so severe that many Christians quietly skip over it: not everyone should be given continued access to what is sacred.
There is a sentence from the mouth of Jesus that sounds almost shocking when you first hear it.

Especially if you have spent years believing that being a good Christian means endlessly explaining yourself, endlessly giving people another chance to mock what you treasure, endlessly reopening doors God may be teaching you to close.
Jesus said:
“Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine…”
Matthew 7:6.
And the sentence becomes even more startling when you see it in the Greek text in which Matthew has been preserved:
“Μὴ δῶτε τὸ ἅγιον τοῖς κυσίν, μηδὲ βάλητε τοὺς μαργαρίτας ὑμῶν ἔμπροσθεν τῶν χοίρων…”
Mē dōte to hagion tois kysin, mēde balēte tous margaritas hymōn emprosthen tōn choirōn…
“Do not give what is holy to the dogs, nor cast your pearls before the pigs…”
The key words are painfully vivid.
ἅγιον — hagion — holy, sacred, set apart.
κυσίν — kysin — dogs.
μαργαρίτας — margaritas — pearls.
χοίρων — choirōn — pigs.
καταπατήσουσιν — katapatēsousin — they will trample them down.
And then comes the frightening conclusion:
“…καὶ στραφέντες ῥήξωσιν ὑμᾶς.”
“…and having turned, they may tear you.”
Jesus was not describing a minor disagreement.

He was painting a picture of something precious being offered where it will not merely be rejected but desecrated—and of the giver eventually being wounded in the process. The underlying Greek of Matthew 7:6 contains precisely this progression: holy thing, dogs; pearls, pigs; trampling; turning; tearing.
And perhaps that is why this verse hurts.
Because some of us know exactly what it feels like to keep placing pearls into hands that only crush them.
You gave someone truth.
They laughed.
You shared what Jesus had done in your life.
They mocked it.
You told someone something sacred about your struggle, your repentance, your marriage, your past, your recovery, your prayers, your wounds…
and later discovered that the thing you whispered through tears became entertainment in another room.
You forgave.
They interpreted forgiveness as permission.
You showed mercy.
They interpreted mercy as weakness.
You opened the door again.
They brought the same destruction back through it.
You explained yourself for the twentieth time to someone who had already decided to misunderstand you.
And somewhere inside you was a frightened Christian conscience saying:
“If I stop, am I being unloving?”
“If I walk away, am I failing Jesus?”
“If I stop arguing, have I abandoned the Gospel?”
“If I create a boundary, does that mean I have not forgiven?”
Then Matthew 7:6 stands in front of us like a locked door we never noticed before.
But be very careful here.
Because this verse has also been terribly abused.
Jesus is not giving Christians permission to walk around deciding which human beings are worthless.
He is not authorizing spiritual arrogance.
He is not telling believers to look at unbelievers with disgust.
And He certainly is not contradicting His command to love our enemies.
Look at what comes immediately before Matthew 7:6.
“Judge not…”
Then Jesus speaks about someone noticing a speck in another person's eye while ignoring the log in his own.
His command is devastatingly personal:
First deal with your own eye.
First confront your own hypocrisy.
First let truth cut you.
First repent.
Then you will be able to see clearly enough to help your brother.
And immediately after warning against hypocritical judgment, Jesus says:
“Do not give dogs what is holy…”
That placement matters.
Matthew 7 does not teach the absence of discernment.
It teaches discernment without hypocrisy.
Before I decide what someone else is doing with holy things, Jesus makes me look into the mirror.
Before I start identifying pigs, I had better start identifying planks.
That changes everything.
Christian discernment begins with repentance.
The proud person says, “Look at those terrible people.”
The disciple says, “Lord, search me first.”
The proud person uses Matthew 7:6 as a weapon.
The disciple receives Matthew 7:1–5 as surgery before ever touching verse 6.
And suddenly one of Jesus’ strangest commands becomes one of His most necessary.
Because love does not require the abandonment of wisdom.
Forgiveness does not mean unlimited access.
Grace does not require you to call evil good.
Compassion does not mean participating in another person's contempt for what is sacred.
And proclaiming Christ does not mean arguing forever with someone who only wants another opportunity to mock Him.
There is a difference between someone who doubts and someone who delights in desecration.
There is a difference between a wounded skeptic and a hardened mocker.
There is a difference between the person saying, “I don't understand,” and the person saying, “Give me another holy thing so I can spit on it.”
Jesus knows the difference.
And He teaches His disciples that there are moments when faithfulness means speaking…
and moments when faithfulness means stopping.
That is difficult for sincere Christians because we desperately want people to be saved.
You have a son who has wandered.
A daughter who no longer believes.
A husband who laughs when you mention church.
A wife who has become cold toward God.
A friend who used to pray beside you and now ridicules everything he once believed.
So you keep talking.
Another sermon.
Another message.
Another video.
Another argument.
Another late-night paragraph.
Another desperate attempt to find exactly the right sentence that will finally break through.
Maybe if I explain it better.
Maybe if I send one more Scripture.
Maybe if I answer one more objection.
Maybe if I defend Christianity one more time.
And sometimes perseverance is exactly what love requires.
But sometimes…
the person is no longer listening.
You are no longer planting.
You are simply supplying more material to be trampled.
There comes a moment when continuing the argument may cease to be faithful witness and become a refusal to accept that only the Holy Spirit can change a heart.
You are not the Savior.
Jesus is.
That sentence may free somebody reading this.
You are not the Savior.
You cannot argue someone into regeneration.
You cannot emotionally manipulate someone into repentance.
You cannot carry somebody into the kingdom on your back.
You can witness.
You can pray.
You can love.
You can answer honestly.
You can live faithfully.
You can proclaim Christ.
You can keep the door of mercy open.
But salvation belongs to God.
And sometimes the most faithful thing you can do is stop fighting the argument and start fighting on your knees.
Pray.
Love them.
Live differently in front of them.
And trust Christ with the person you cannot change.
That does not mean abandoning people.
It means refusing to confuse relentless argument with relentless love.
There is another side of this command, however, and it cuts even deeper.
Maybe the person trampling the pearl…
has been you.
Maybe you have treated holy things casually.
Maybe the Gospel became background noise.
Maybe “Jesus died for me” became so familiar that it stopped astonishing you.
Maybe grace became an excuse instead of a miracle.
Maybe you knew the Scriptures well enough to quote them while secretly protecting the very sin those Scriptures condemned.
Maybe worship played in your headphones while pornography remained hidden in your browser history.
Maybe your Bible sat beside the bed while bitterness slept inside your heart.
Maybe everyone at church thought you were strong.
But God knew.
God saw the private messages.
The secret addiction.
The jealousy.
The resentment.
The affair nobody discovered.
The money nobody knew about.
The compromise you renamed “struggle” because “sin” sounded too uncomfortable.
The prayerlessness.
The coldness.
The double life.
And perhaps the terrifying question is no longer:
“Who are the dogs and pigs?”
Perhaps the question becomes:
“What have I done with the holy things God placed in my hands?”
That is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Christianity is not the story of respectable people looking down on filthy people.
Christianity is the story of sinners being rescued by a holy Savior.
Every Christian comes to Jesus empty-handed.
No résumé.
No moral trophy.
No religious performance capable of purchasing forgiveness.
Just sin.
Need.
Repentance.
And mercy.
We were not rescued because we deserved the Pearl.
We were rescued because Christ is merciful.
Jesus walked toward people stained by scandal.
Tax collectors.
Sexually broken people.
Religious hypocrites willing to repent.
Outcasts.
Failures.
Cowards.
People with histories they could not erase.
And ultimately He walked toward a cross.
There the Holy One was mocked.
Stripped.
Rejected.
Crucified.
The hands that healed were pierced.
The mouth that spoke life was mocked.
The King wore thorns.
And the One who had no scandal of His own carried the shame of sinners.
This is why grace should never become cheap to us.
Forgiveness cost blood.
Not ours.
His.
And resurrection declared that scandal does not have to write the final chapter.
Peter's denial did not write his final chapter.
The thief's crimes did not write his final chapter.
The shame of sinners who come to Christ does not write their final chapter.
Jesus does.
This is the heartbeat of everything we mean when we say:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not because Jesus pretends sin never happened.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Not because holiness no longer matters.
Jesus rewrites lives precisely by confronting sin, forgiving repentant sinners, giving new hearts, and calling redeemed people into a transformed way of living.
Grace is not God saying your sin was insignificant.
Grace is God revealing how serious sin was—and then showing you the scars of the Savior who paid its price.
So perhaps Matthew 7:6 is not merely about protecting pearls from other people.
Perhaps it should make us ask whether we ourselves still recognize the value of the Pearl.
Do you still tremble at the Gospel?
Does the cross still humble you?
Does forgiveness still astonish you?
Does the name of Jesus still mean more than religious vocabulary?
Or have holy things become ordinary?
There are people begging God for the Bible you barely open.
There are people longing for Christian fellowship while we casually neglect it.
There are people discovering Jesus with tears in their eyes while some of us have heard His name for decades without being moved.
Familiarity can become dangerous when familiarity produces contempt.
Do not trample what heaven calls holy.
Do not trade eternal treasure for temporary appetite.
Do not exchange Christ for the thing that will entertain you tonight and accuse you tomorrow morning.
Do not sell a pearl for another handful of mud.
And if you have already done it…
come home.
That is the Gospel.
Not “clean yourself up enough for Jesus.”
Come home.
Repent.
Confess.
Turn.
Believe.
The same Jesus who warns us about trampling holy things is the Jesus who receives sinners who turn to Him.
Your worst chapter does not have authority over Christ's ability to redeem.
Your hidden sin is not hidden from Him.
Your shame does not frighten Him.
Your past does not surprise Him.
But grace is not permission to remain buried.
Come into the light.
Somebody reading this has been pretending for too long.
You know exactly what God has been confronting.
You have postponed obedience because tomorrow always sounded easier than today.
But tomorrow is not promised.
Jesus is calling now.
Not to perform.
Not to impress Christians.
Not to manufacture tears.
To repent.
To trust Him.
To surrender what you keep defending.
Maybe your prayer tonight needs only a few words:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
And if this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not have to tell strangers every detail. But you can stop pretending.
If you are exhausted but refusing to abandon Christ, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If your soul has been running on empty and you need believers to pray with you, simply comment, “pray for me.”
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded believer needed tonight.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The person who has been quietly falling apart.
The person whose Facebook posts look normal but whose life you know has been heavy.
The friend drifting from Christ.
The believer drowning in shame.
The skeptic who has sincere questions.
The person who needs to discover that Christianity is not about polishing sinners until they look religious, but about sinners being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Send it privately if their pain deserves privacy.
You can love someone without giving endless access to what they repeatedly desecrate.
You can forgive without calling destruction healthy.
You can stop an argument without stopping prayer.
You can guard what is sacred without becoming self-righteous.
And you can discover that sometimes silence is not cowardice.
Sometimes silence says:

“I have told you about Jesus. I love you. I will pray for you. My door is open when you sincerely want truth. But I will no longer turn the name of Christ into entertainment for an argument you have no intention of hearing.”
That is not hatred.
That can be discernment.
And when the person finally comes back broken and asking honest questions?
Do not stand at the door reminding them how badly they behaved.
Remember how Christ received you.
Bring the Gospel.
Bring mercy.
Bring truth.
Bring Jesus.
Because the goal was never to protect pearls so fiercely that sinners could never encounter grace.
The goal is to recognize the Pearl's worth.

If Gospel Warrior has helped you treasure Christ more deeply, consider staying close to this work. Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelievers to follow as well.
But hear this clearly, because biblical integrity matters more than conversion numbers:
You cannot purchase God's blessing.
It cannot purchase forgiveness.
It cannot purchase answered prayer.
And Gospel Warrior should never replace your local church, your responsibility toward your family, or generosity God has called you to elsewhere.
Scripture teaches giving from the heart rather than giving produced by pressure: “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
He will not.
Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, reaching, building, and placing Christ-centered resources in front of people who may encounter them during the darkest night of their lives.
And financial support is not the only way to help.
Sharing matters.
Maybe you never know who.
Maybe there is no comment.
No dramatic testimony.
No message thanking you.
But perhaps somebody sitting alone at 2:13 in the morning sees what you shared…
reads…
stops…
weeps…
and prays for the first time in years.
You may never know this side of eternity.
Share anyway.
The mission is bigger than merchandise.
Bigger than engagement.
Bigger than algorithms.
If any of those things ever become the treasure, we have missed the message of Matthew 7:6 ourselves.
Jesus is the treasure.
The Gospel is the message.
People are the mission field.
Grace is the miracle.
Transformation is the evidence.
And God's glory is the goal.
Follow so we can keep walking through difficult Scriptures together.
And never forget the strange warning that began all of this.
“Do not give dogs what is holy.”
Jesus never told us that because holy things are worthless.
He told us because they are precious.
So guard what Christ calls sacred.
But never let guarding the pearl make your heart hard toward the person who does not yet recognize its value.
You once needed mercy too.
You still do.
Perhaps the person who mocks Christ today will worship Him tomorrow.
Perhaps the person who trampled the pearl will one day discover what it was worth.
Perhaps the prodigal you finally stopped arguing with will someday come home.
So discern without hatred.
Set boundaries without vengeance.
Speak truth without pride.
Forgive without becoming foolish.
Walk away when wisdom requires it.
Return with mercy when repentance opens the door.
And through everything…
keep your eyes on Jesus.
Because the greatest tragedy is not that somebody once threw a pearl into the mud.
The greatest tragedy would be standing so close to the Pearl of greatest price that you could touch Him…
and never realizing what you had been given.
Do not spend your life fighting over pearls and wake up one day to discover that you stopped treasuring Christ.
